current_episode.title: EP 125: The PR Launch That Cleared The Building

guest.titre_secondaire: PR Lecturer and Former Agency Leader
guest.bio_context: Fellow of the CIPR and former president of the Chartered Institute of Journalists with over 20 years of teaching PR experience. Started his career as a journalist in the late 1960s, then joined Townsend Taurus as a shipping company PR professional, later worked at Burson Marsteller from 1979 where he managed major accounts including cruise lines and royal patronage. Diagnosed with stage four prostate cancer in May 2024, he now dedicates his work exclusively to voluntary positions with charities and NHS trusts, including Yorkshire Cancer Research, Hope for Tomorrow, and stroke charities.

context.real_quote: Honesty and integrity are on the wall but the industry does not have that. It's not the default position.

context.transcript_excerpt: Welcome back to Embracing Marketing Mistakes, the show that teaches you growth from failure. I'm Chris Norton and joined as ever by Will Ockendon and today we have a guest I've been looking forward to speaking to for a very long time. He's a fellow of the CIPR, a former president of the Chartered Institute of Journalists and one of the most outspoken ethical voices the industry actually has. Here is the twist that makes today fun though. He taught PR for over two decades and now one of his former students gets to dig through the past and ask the really awkward questions. I know you guys are going to enjoy this. There's tons of value here today and some of the mistakes are gold. So sit back, get a coffee and enjoy. So Robert Vincent Taylor, welcome to the show. Thank you very much. I'm delighted to be here. So we've got a description here of you as the PR veteran, former journalist, agency leader and PR lecturer of more than 20 years. So what are you doing today in your day-to-day? My world changed in May 2024 when I was sitting in front of an oncologist who told me I had six years to live because I had stage four prostate cancer and that really turned my life upside down as it would for most people. But I was then 77 and it changed my life. So now, in a way, all my work is for voluntary work and if I get paid, I put it straight back into charities. So I don't take anything for myself except for travel expenses. So I now work for as a public governor at Airedale NHS Trust and as you know, the NHS is going through humongous changes and problems. They're building a £1.5 billion new hospital. It's one of the seven hospitals being built in the country but we don't know what's finalising design and everything else and that's really exciting. And I work for Yorkshire Cancer Research and I know you've done some work with them. They're fantastic. And I work for stroke charities. I help put together a thing called All Things Stroke for people who are sufferers of stroke, patients and relatives so in plain English so people could understand the condition and particularly if they were still working and how they get back into work. And we were just discussing our mutual friend, Andy Green, so I'm going to be sending him things he can look at in his hospital bed about how to recover from that. And I work for prostate cancer. I do stuff for a thing called Hope for Tomorrow. They run the mobile, they look like F1 motorhomes for Formula 1 and motor racing but they've been adapted for mobile treatment centres. They're fantastic. They really are fantastic so I work with them too. So basically I'm an offshoot of their corporate comms department because charities don't have any money and the last thing they're spending is on marketing and PR and the charity you work for which is fantastic, Yorkshire Cancer Research. So I just take off them stuff they don't have the arms and legs to do and I get a lot of enjoyment from that. I'm not a physical guy. I'm walking around the hills even though I live in the countryside, albeit with a station. I need to keep my mind active otherwise I just get very depressed. So you joined the PR profession agency side in the 70s, is that right? So what was that like and how has it changed since the 70s? Well I started life as a journalist. I trained in the late 1960s when they were still selling type by hand and then I joined a company called Townsend Taurus and it was a bit like the Ryanair of today. All the ships were called Free Enterprise 1, Free Enterprise 2, 3, 4, 5 but they had that catastrophic disaster. They held a free enterprise and they were an interesting company. They were fast and furious and I spent six years working with them and I learned everything about how to organize an event. Like you walk the event. You don't just write it down. pending_qa.q: What went wrong with the Burger King menu launch event at a fancy hotel?
pending_qa.r: Robert organized a reception at a hotel to showcase Burger King's new flame-grilled menu with a professional chef in full regalia. However, the hotel served Coca-Cola at the bar afterward when Burger King's official partner was Pepsi at that time. The client was shocked and said 'this is unbelievable, do your homework.' Robert had not instructed the hotel on the Pepsi requirement, and the account was not held much longer after this incident.
